Commercial radio and television satisfy most of this requirement. Collectively, they are known as Broadcast Communications. They are controlled by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), and established operating guidelines for maximum efficiency....

Even though cable television reaches millions of homes across the United States and other parts of the world, local television broadcast stations are still necessary for those who rely on antennas for television reception...

AM and FM radio provide music, news, weather, sports, traffic conditions and other programming that might not be available otherwise. Occasionally, special events are aired in simulcast; that is, a live event will be broadcast on both radio and television simultaneously..
Television, radio and satellites are the types of broadcast systems discussed in this lesson.

A broadcast system can be defined as any communications system (audio, video, data, or image) designed for point-to-multipoint transmissions. This means that one transmitter is providing communications to many users. The word broadcast means to send out in all directions...
DISCUSSION

There is also point-to-point service where the transmission is intended for only one receiver. Examples of this type include remote locations such as fire-ranger towers or mobile users like traveling appliance repair trucks. This lesson will not cover this type of transmission...

Except for the most remote places on the planet, the airways are filled with radio waves. Radios allow us to have two-way communications between our homes and cars, boats, or airplanes. We can even communicate with people who are on the space shuttle or exploring the moon...

Until the process of superimposing a low-frequency (long-wave) voice information component on a high-frequency (short-wave) carrier signal was perfected, the most widely used form of communications was a system based on the transmission of a continuous-wave (CW) signal...

With this system, the signal was interrupted periodically (Morse code) to produce a coded message. The CW system required tremendous training and expertise on the part of the persons involved in transmitting and receiving the messages, and therefore the field was limited to a few experts...
With the development of modulation, a whole new era of communications evolved, the results of which can be seen all around us today.

Most of us are familiar with the AM ( amplitude modulated) and FM (frequency modulated) broadcast stations whether we listen to them at home, at work, or in our automobiles. Regular radio broadcasts began in the 1920s at station KDKA in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Amplitude modulation was the method used first...

Each station is assigned a carrier frequency by the FCC. AM broadcasts use 540 to 1650 kHz, while FM broadcasts are assigned 88 to 108 MHz. Without this assignment, the air waves would be filled with overlapping transmissions, resulting in an unintelligible racket. Radio receivers have tuning circuits to allow only the reception of the desired station....
AM stations are allotted a bandwidth of 10 kHz. FM stations occupy a 200 kHz bandwidth. Frequency modulation occurred in 1939 and the first FM stereo broadcast was available in 1961.

FM systems have several advantages over AM. They are inherently less noisy due to the type of modulation used and are capable of broadcasting a broader range of audio frequencies for better fidelity...

Radio transmitters send messages into the air at a specific frequency in the spectrum. All radio frequency electromagnetic signals change polarity (go from positive to negative) on a regular basis. This polarity change defines their frequency, which is measured in cycles per second. One cycle per second is called one hertz.....

The hertz was named after a German physicist Heinrich Hertz who in 1887 demonstrated the effect of electromagnetic radiation through space.h signals travel differently through the atmosphere. The correct wavelength needs to be chosen for each type of radio communication...

All electromagnetic waves travel through free space at the same speed. Light is a form of electromagnetic wave. Radio and light waves travel at about 186,000 miles per second, which is about 300 million meters per second. Thus, a wave sent by a radio transmitter is 186,000 miles or 300 million meters away one second later.....

This is true no matter what the frequency of the wave is. During that same second, the radio transmitter generates the number of wave cycles defined by its frequency. Thus, a 10 MHz transmitter will generate 10 million cycles in one second. These 10 million cycles cover 300 million meters in one second...
Therefore, the wavelength, or distance covered by one cycle, is: Wavelength = 300 million meters per second/ 10 million cycles per second = 30 meters.

Radio signals with low frequencies have long wavelengths and radio signals with high frequencies have short wavelengths. Different wavelength signals travel differently through the atmosphere. The correct wavelength needs to be chosen for each type of radio communication...

For example, low frequency (LF) and high frequency (HF) radio waves bounce off the atmosphere's upper layer, the ionosphere. This permits long-distance communication between two points on earth. Super high frequency (SHF) radio waves are used for satellite communication because they travel straight through the ionosphere.....

A basic radio broadcasting system consists of a transmitter, a receiver, an antenna for each, and a channel. The distance of transmission for a wireless communication system can be less than a mile or as much as 5,000 miles, depending on the type of service...

Radio transmitters are normally on top of large towers or placed atop tall buildings or hills to promote greater broadcast coverage. Some stations that provide coverage for a large area use repeater stations. Repeater stations are receiver/transmitter combinations that first receive the weakening signal, then reshape and amplify it before re-transmitting it.....

Radio receivers found in automobiles and home entertainment systems are capable of receiving, almost exclusively, the broadcast AM and FM bands only. Since these two bands are the purest form of broadcast radio and what the majority of people use, it makes sense. They are used mainly for entertainment but they also provide public service to communities.....
Few people spend time listening to 24 hour NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) weather broadcasts or the latest headline news from Antarctica.

However, there are several other broadcast transmission bands that common home receivers cannot discern because they use a different frequency band, or because a different modulation format is employed. Still, the signals are available to anyone with the receiving equipment designed for the frequency bands and modulation forms.....

Multiple band receivers are commercially available and are reasonably inexpensive. Some more expensive models have the ability to receive single sideband and narrow-band FM transmissions. These transmissions are mostly voice communication bands used by police, emergency services, and the military, etc....

Police, fire, other emergency services, taxi companies, weather, citizen's band (CB) radio, the military, and short wave (HAM) all send radio signals into the airwaves. These transmissions occur day and night, but there are periods of inactivity...

Amateur radio is one of the largest noncommercial radio services in the world. Amateur operators, also called hams communicate with each other using Morse code, voice, radio teletype, slow-scan television, and digital communications...

Public service is a large part of amateur radio but it is also used for entertainment. Hams often provide emergency communications in times of national disaster such as flooding, tornadoes, hurricanes, and earthquakes...

Citizen's band radio is another noncommercial radio service, which can be used by the general public. The CB band has forty 10-kHz channels extending from 26.965 MHz up to 27.405 MHz. The CB band allows a maximum power output of 4 watts. Unlike amateur radio, no license is required by the FCC to operate a CB radio.....

Most of these radio transmissions are categorized as communications radio and contain only voice transmissions as opposed to music programming formats found in the commercial AM and FM bands. Some radio broadcasts are now being transmitted by cable in the same fashion as broadcast television.nnn
The word television means to see at a distance. Broadcast television began officially in 1941 but did not become popular until 1945. Our present color television system was adopted in 1953...

For a while, the big three TV networks (ABC, CBS and NBC) were really all there were to be received on the television airways. These stations transmitted in the very-high frequency (VHF) range. Soon thereafter, a handful of ultra-high frequency (UHF) stations followed...
Each television station occupies a bandwidth of 6 MHz, which is 600 times more than an AM broadcast station and 30 times more than an FM station.

Television transmitters have a limited useful range. The broadcast power emitted from the transmitting antenna is determined by the FCC and is based upon several factors including the terrain and the proximity of other transmitters...

To provide service to people who live beyond the range of the nearest transmitter, cable TV systems have been installed. In a cable system, the primary transmitter (of a broad cast station) sends the signal to a local cable company who disseminates the signal to homes and businesses via wire.

Cable TV systems have been built in most metropolitan areas, even where regular television reception is good because programming other than broadcast TV can be added to the cable. This programming includes movies, sporting events, concerts, and community news...

While scores of other stations are now available through cable, broadcast stations are still the only source of free public programming. Even though the programming from a broadcast station may be received through cable, it is still considered a broadcast station...

The transmission of a television signal is a very complex procedure that requires in-depth studies. In a radio or television broadcasting system, the transmitter sends out electromagnetic radio waves from its antenna. At the receiving end, an antenna picks up or intercepts the transmitted signal. The receiver reproduces the transmitted information.....

Since the signal received by a television receiver provides both audio and video, the television transmitter is actually two transmitters in one. Two separate carrier waves are used in the transmission of a television signal: one for the picture and one for the sound....

The video component is amplitude modulated and the audio component is frequency modulated. Initially, the audio and video are separated so that they can be used to modulate their respective carriers. Once the modulation process is complete, the two components of the signal are combined and transmitted as one composite signal....

The television receiver is, for the most part, a television transmitter in reverse. Its purpose is to receive the broadcast signal, separate the audio and video signals from their carrier frequencies, and reproduce the original picture and sound...

Since all television transmissions traveling through space in the area of any given television antenna may be received, the receiver must have a tuning section that allows the user to select a particular channel. For each channel selected, the tuning section allows only the frequency associated with that channel to be processed and displayed on the screen.....
The tuning section consists of an RF amplifier, a mixer, and a local oscillator.

Satellite is a form of broadcast television that requires a special high frequency receiver that has the ability to receive carrier frequencies in the gigahertz range and down-convert them to a frequency that a television receiver can use...

Some homes have satellite receivers that enable the user to receive television broadcasting through a dish antenna. Initially, they were large in both size and expense. Advances in technology have brought the prices down so many people can afford them.

In some cases, the equipment and installation are offered free with a contract to pay for programming for some period of time. most cases, the monthly fee is equal to or less than the average cable television bill.erage cable television bill...
This particular type of broadcasting is used mainly for home entertainment. Satellites also transmit other forms of communications such as telephone and government communications...

The receiving station consist of a high-gain parabolic antenna, a highly sensitive receiver, and a frequency converter. Frequency converters are used to convert GHz signals to lower radio frequency signals that can be used by the ground equipment...

The two main aspects of satellite control are orientation control and position control. Orientation control is required for initial orientation and for antenna adjustments. Adjustments are necessary to keep the antenna constantly viewing the earth and the solar cells viewing the sun...
COMMUNICATIONS
SUPPORT SUBSYSTEMS

Position control is required for initial satellite emplacement and to compensate for forces that tend to divert the satellite from its orbit. Such forces include gravitational action from the sun and moon and solar radiation pressure. Solar radiation pressure is a result of solar wind. As it encounters matter, it exerts a physical force or pressure.....

Some orientation and position control systems are completely contained within the satellite and require no outside control. Other control systems allow ground controllers access to the control loop, which affords more flexibility...
Communication satellites are really radio relay stations called repeaters. They are located high above the earth so its signals can be picked up over a very large area.

Telephone and television broadcast signals are beamed up to the satellite from an earth station by using a large, highly directive microwave dish antenna that is synchronized to the satellite position. This is called an up-link. The carrier frequency of the up-link normally ranges from 5.92 to 6.43 GHz...

The satellite's transponder down-converts these signals and returns them to earth. The returned signals are called the down-link and range from 3.7 to 4.2 GHz. To prevent the transponder's strong transmitted signal from interfering with the earth station's weak received signal, the carrier frequencies are separated by about 2 GHz.....

A transponder is a device that receives the weak microwave signal, amplifies and conditions it, and re-transmits the signal back to another earth station in a different location. Anyone with a satellite receiver in the coverage area can receive the transmission. Some systems now allow inexpensive direct home reception of satellite broadcasts.....

Communication satellites appear to hover over given areas above the equator. This does not make stationary, but rather geostationary. They have the same angular velocity as the Earth. (i.e., one complete cycle per 24 hours), and so they appear to be stationed over one spot on the globe.....

Whether to use a stationary satellite or a succession of satellites in low, elliptical orbits for global communications was a question pondered by the communication engineers in the early 1960s. Satellites in close elliptical orbits require relatively low transmitting powers, and receiver sensitivities but must be tracked by the antennas of the ground stations.....
Ibaraki POS satellite earth station. (Tokyo)
Stationary satellites present no tracking problems but are so far away that they require large antennas, high power transmissions and high receiver sensitivity. This was the method chosen.
Another use for satellites is the Global Positioning System (GPS). It provides exact positioning information in terms of latitude, longitude, elevation, and time to those who have a receiver..

GPS works on the principle of triangulation. By knowing the distance from three or more satellites, a receiver can calculate its position by solving a set of equations. Information from three satellites is needed to calculate longitude and latitude at a known elevation; four satellites are needed to include altitude...

In theory, the distance from satellite to receiver can be calculated by multiplying the time it takes for the signal to arrive by the speed at which it travels (the speed of light). In practice, more sophisticated calculations are required to account for the fact that receiver clocks are not as accurate as satellite clocks..
Distance = Signal arrival time x Speed of lightttttttttttt

The application of this technology is useful to both the general public and to governments. It is especially important to the military that use the information to pinpoint the location of troops and to obtain targeting information for tactical missiles, field artillery, etc. Satellites provide real-time (as it's occurring) intelligence.....

GPS was designed for and is operated by the U.S. Military even though it is also used by the civilian arms of the government as well as the general populace. GPS has many uses such as navigation and land surveying. Since it is a technology of military significance, two types of codes emanate from the GPS satellites.....

One is a C/A (Coarse Acquisition) code for commercial or private use, and the other is a P (Precise) code used by the military. The P code is far more accurate and can be encrypted to prohibit unauthorized receivers from understanding the information being transmitted...

The SPACE SEGMENT is made up of 24 satellites that orbit the earth every twelve hours at an altitude of 10,900 miles, repeatedly broadcasting their position and the time. The atomic clocks aboard each satellite keeps time by the vibration of atoms and are accurate to one second in 30 years...

Most of the time, there are more than 24 GPS satellites in space at any given time because replacements for older satellites are normally launched in advance. This prevents any lapse in the system's operation...

The satellites are placed in orbit so that they repeat approximately the same ground track once every 24 hours. The satellite positioning creates six orbital planes with normally four satellites in each plane...

incline with respect to earth's equator. This coverage provides users with line-of-sight for five to eight satellites from any point on earth. All GPS receivers need direct and unobstructed line of sight access to each satellite.....

The CONTROL SEGMENT comprises a network of tracking stations at various locations around the world. The primary station is called the MASTER CONTROL and is centered at Schriever Air Force Base in Colorado......

Monitor stations measure the satellite signals and load them into computer models for each satellite. The computers develop precise orbital data and time corrections for the satellites. This information is sent to the Master Control station and uploaded to the satellites, which in turn, send the information to the GPS receivers.....

The USER SEGMENT consists of the GPS receivers and the user community. The GPS navigation receivers are available for ships, aircraft, terrestrial vehicles, and small hand-held devices for individuals. The receivers convert the satellite signals into position, velocity, and time approximations.......

In order to provide the four dimensions X, Y, Z (position) and time for some given object in some given space, four satellites are required. The graphic only visualizes positional planes X, Y and Z...
Single receivers can provide information accurate to about

100 feet. When two receivers are available, more information that is precise can be obtained. To do this, one receiver is dedicated to a point already established while the other (the one whose location is sought), processes the same satellite data and resolves positional error through parallax correction..

Parallax correction takes into account the apparent change in the position of an object resulting from the change in the direction or position from which it is viewed. This process can bring accuracy to within a fraction of an inch...
